source.title: Panda: A pretrained forecast model for chaotic dynamics
source.authors: Jeffrey Lai; Anthony Bao; William Gilpin

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports scaling results for chaotic-dynamics forecasting, but does not test language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling, extrapolation of such losses, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its forecast-error scaling measures a different outcome.
record.gate_note: The paper cites neural-language-model scaling work and explicitly distinguishes its experiment from traditional neural scaling laws. Its own scaling results concern forecast error in dynamical systems, not language-model pretraining loss. Those related results are recorded with versions ["none"]. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains and evaluates Panda, a forecasting model for chaotic dynamics. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss of language models. Its 'dynamical systems scaling law' (Sec 5.3, Fig 5) varies the diversity of training systems at a fixed number of total timepoints. The authors state it is distinct from Kaplan-style scaling, and the text gives no power-law fit or exponent. The model-size runs in Appendix K (42M and 72M) also change training iterations and dataset, have only two or three points, and fit no power law. So none of V1–V7 is tested. V5 (power-law form in other modalities) is the closest, but neither a power-law form nor a clean parameter, data or compute sweep is established. Both findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors report that zero-shot forecast performance scales with the number of unique dynamical systems at fixed total timepoints. They call this distinct from traditional neural scaling laws for total data, and tie it to dynamical-systems theory. They also report that the scaled-up checkpoints improve, without fitting a law.
record.recipe_differences: The study concerns pretrained forecasting models for chaotic dynamical systems, not language-model loss scaling. Its diversity experiment varies unique systems at fixed total timepoints; its model-size runs also change training duration and dataset.
record.method_sensitivity: The diversity experiment varies the number of unique systems and initial conditions at fixed total timepoints. The scaled-up runs also change training iterations and training datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed number of total training timepoints, zero-shot forecast error on 9.3e3 held-out systems falls as the number of unique training systems rises from about 156 to about 2e4 (Fig 5). The text gives no fitted exponent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For chaotic-dynamics forecasters, diversity of training systems at fixed data volume improves zero-shot generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Panda 72M (800K iterations, 8-IC mixed-period data) has lower median sMAPE and MAE than Panda 42M (400K iterations, improved data) at all horizons. Model size is confounded with data and training length.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger Panda checkpoints trained with more data and iterations forecast chaotic systems more accurately.

record.problems: The paper does not test language-model loss scaling. The diversity-scaling plot's numerical values are not present in the text. The scaled-up model runs differ in dataset and training duration as well as parameter count, so the effect of parameter count alone cannot be determined.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of power laws fitted on small runs to larger runs.
Compute-optimal split between parameters and tokens.
Effect of architecture shape at a fixed parameter count. The patch-length ablation in Appendix J is not a depth/width test at fixed N.
A power-law form of loss in a non-text domain. Panda model-size runs are confounded with data and iteration changes, and no power law is fitted.
Downstream predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of exponents or allocation on setup or fitting choices.

missing.what: Panda 21M original median sMAPE (27.6/36.7/46.3) and MAE (0.35/0.49/0.65) at horizons 128/256/512. These are the smallest point of the model-size comparison. The 21M-improved checkpoint appears only in Fig 23.
missing.locator: Appendix D, Tables 8 and 9; Appendix K, Fig 23

record.verdict_notes: The abstract claims 'a neural scaling law for differential equations', but no power-law fit is reported in the text. Rows r1–r8 were marked 'observed' individually even though their values are figure-only; they are changed to cannot_determine. The reader's relation (discusses) and tranche (T6) are kept.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict substantially larger runs.
The compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture-shape effects on language-model held-out pretraining loss.

Whether the same power-law form for held-out pretraining loss holds in other modalities or training regimes. The paper reports forecast-error scaling in dynamical systems, but does not establish the same power-law form.
Predictability of downstream language-model task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Whether language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation depend on setup or fitting choices, or whether the language-model curves bend away from power laws.
